newsitem.title: THAILAND: PRESS DIGEST - Thai newspapers - Jan 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Thai newspapers - Jan 7.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Thai press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Former Parliament president Ukrit Mongkolnavin has quit the Constitution Drafting Assembly (CDA) and dropped a bombshell with his prediction that the political reform process will be nothing but deception and a waste of time. His departure enhances former House speaker Uthai Pimchaichon's chances of being elected CDA president in today's meeting. (THE NATION) (BANGKOK POST)

- Thai Airways International has been told to shelve its 28-billion-baht plan to buy aircraft and the military to stall some defence projects to cut the current account deficit to 7.2 percent of GDP. The prime minister says he expects a package of economies to bring about a one-percent cut in the deficit registered last year at 8.2 percent, or 335,700 million baht. (BANGKOK POST)

- Thai border and provincial police have been reinforced along sections of the southern border to prevent a possible influx of foreign workers deported by Malaysia. A senior immigration police officer says Thailand will not let Malaysia push illegal foreign workers over the border again. Malaysia has deported hundreds of Burmese and Bangladeshi workers to Thailand, from where they sneaked into Malaysia. (THE NATION)

- The Bank of Thailand has played down ratings assigned to four Thai banks by Standard and Poor's (S&P) because appropiate measures have been taken to solve the problems in the banking sector. The central bank says the ratings will not cause any impact to Thai financial institutions because the analysis was made without enough understanding of the true picture of the Thai economy. (BUSINESS DAY)

- Rampant oil smuggling last year could have cost the government up to nine billion baht in lost tax revenues, with one industry estimate putting the volume of illegal oil entering the country at 50,000 barrels per day. Senior executives of legitimate oil firms have been monitoring the illegal operations and insist diesel oil smuggling has remained high despite government crackdowns. (BANGKOK POST)

- Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh has sent a signal to the top authorities at the Commerce Ministry and the Bank of Thailand that prices this year should not be allowed to rise so high as to affect the competitiveness of Thai exports. In addition, Chavalit wants the ministry to curb the flow of imports, especially in categories which rarely have an effect on the Thai export sector, such as passenger cars and luxury goods, to ease the country's trade deficit which might possibly rise by 30 per cent by the end of this year. (THE NATION)
